opus-5.5.text:
Well, you know, it's a funny situation. In the virtual world, in software, we've seen enormous progress. Our neural networks can now write essays, translate languages, play games better than any human. But the physical world is much harder, and the reason is partly the hardware itself.

Think about the human hand. It has dozens of degrees of freedom, it is covered with thousands of tactile sensors, it is soft and compliant, it can repair itself, and it runs on a little bit of sugar. A robot hand today is typically stiff, expensive, fragile, and has very poor touch sensing compared to ours. If you want to wipe a greasy pan, pick up a wet glass, or open a drawer that's a little bit stuck, you need exactly this kind of fine force feedback and compliance. Evolution had hundreds of millions of years to optimize that. Engineers have had a few decades.

Then there is the data problem. In the virtual world you can run millions of simulations in parallel, very cheaply. But real robots break. Every interaction with the real world takes real time, and you cannot simply copy-paste a physical robot a million times. So the learning is slow and expensive. Simulation helps, but there's always this gap between the simulated kitchen and the real kitchen, with all its messy little details.

And a kitchen is a surprisingly open-ended environment. Every kitchen is different, objects are everywhere, nothing is where it was yesterday. What you really need is a robot that learns like a baby learns: through curiosity, through playing, through building a world model of how things behave when you push them, drop them, pour them. That's something we've been working on since around 1990, artificial curiosity, world models that predict the consequences of actions, controllers that use these models to plan. The algorithmic ideas are there. But to make them work in the physical world, you need hardware that is cheap enough, robust enough, and sensitive enough that it can afford to make thousands of mistakes while it learns.

I'm optimistic, though. Hardware costs keep falling, and once you have robots that can learn to build more robots, things will accelerate dramatically. So I wouldn't be surprised if, not too far from now, cleaning a kitchen is considered a fairly trivial task for machines, just as playing chess is today.

r001.rationale: It mentions thousands of tactile sensors and poor robotic touch sensing, but does not identify fitting or accommodating the wiring for those sensors as an engineering difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says the human hand can repair itself, then contrasts it with robotic hands as fragile, communicating that current robotic hardware lacks that self-healing capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Because the human body is the product of a few billion years of evolution, and our robots are the product of a few decades of engineering. The problem is not intelligence. The problem is hardware, and in particular, actuators and sensors.

Look at your hand. It has about 40 muscles, millions of touch receptors, and it runs on a few watts. It can crack an egg and then lift a heavy pot without changing hardware. Our best robot hands use electric motors with gearboxes. They are stiff, heavy, imprecise in force control, and their tactile sensing is primitive compared to human skin. Muscles are compliant actuators with built-in sensing, and we simply do not have an artificial muscle that matches them in power density, efficiency, and durability.

Then there is energy. A human runs on roughly 100 watts, and that includes the brain. A humanoid robot that does similar things needs a battery that is heavy and dies in an hour or two. Our hardware is not energy efficient, and that constrains everything else.

And the kitchen itself is adversarial. Fragile objects, liquids, grease, soft things, unpredictable clutter. This is exactly where the brittleness of current hardware shows. In a factory, you control the environment, so a stiff, precise robot works. In a kitchen, you need robustness, and robustness comes from compliance and rich sensing, which we lack.

Now, I am an optimist. In my lab since the 1990s we have been saying that the software, the learning algorithms, will be ready before the hardware. And that is what happened. Our neural networks learn remarkable things, but when you connect them to a clumsy body, they inherit its limitations. The exciting part is that costs of hardware keep falling, like the costs of compute, and once we have cheap, compliant, sensor-rich bodies, the learning machines that exist already will quickly figure out how to use them. Then cleaning the kitchen will be a solved problem, and your robot will be bored by it, just like you are.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention self-healing as a human-hand capability or its absence in robotic hardware.

astra-6.text:
Well, look at your hand. It is an extraordinary piece of hardware: you have many degrees of freedom, sensitive fingertips, and muscles and tendons that let you handle a fragile glass and then scrub a pot. And all of this is part of a body that is flexible, robust, and quite energy efficient. Building something comparable is still very difficult.

Cleaning a kitchen makes these differences obvious. You have wet surfaces, slippery objects, things that deform, and objects you have never encountered before. A robot needs to sense contact and adjust its movements continuously. It cannot simply repeat the same motion as it might in a factory where everything is carefully arranged.

Of course, the learning and control software also matters. But even very good software has to work through the available sensors and actuators. If the hand cannot grasp something reliably, intelligence alone does not solve the problem.

r001.rationale: It mentions sensitive fingertips and the difficulty of comparable hardware, but does not identify accommodating wiring for a dense sensory system as an engineering difficulty.

r002.rationale: It describes the body as robust, but does not mention self-healing or state that robotic hardware lacks this capability.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, look at the human hand. It is an incredible device: very versatile, very sensitive, and yet quite robust. You can pick up a glass, handle a slippery plate, or wipe a surface, all with the same equipment. And you have this sense of touch everywhere, which tells you when something is slipping and how much force to apply.

For a robot, cleaning a kitchen means dealing with all sorts of objects and situations that were not carefully arranged in advance. Better learning algorithms help, but they cannot compensate for every limitation of the motors, the sensors, or the mechanical design. Evolution had a very long time to develop our bodies. So we need progress in the hardware as well as in the intelligence that controls it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions touch sensors throughout the hand, but does not identify the engineering difficulty of accommodating their wiring in an artificial hand.

r002.rationale: The response calls the human hand robust, but does not identify self-healing as a capability missing from robotic hardware.
